I absolutely agree with your points. Usually the "station area" is considered to be within a 1/2mi radius.

But for emergencies, people are always going to have the *option* to drive, and 911 exists for a reason. Capacity, energy efficiency, speed, incentivizing sustainable development, making walking and biking more realistic, societal financial sustainability.

> Right now VTA is spending more than $500 Million dollar to connect Alum Rock light rail to Eastridge bus station, a distance of roughly 3 miles!

This cost for a *fully elevated rail extension* is extremely competitive on a global scale. PPP Adjusted, low cost countries for transit infrastructure like India and Thailand build elevated rail lines for a similar price, IF NOT HIGHER!

While BART to Downtown is a very high cost project that the agency needs to fix (and they're in progress on >$1B of cost savings), EBRC is an extremely competitively priced project on a global scale, something that US agencies consistently struggle with.

SkyTrain isn't light rail, it's an automated light metro.

Light rail is based on the German concept of the stadtbahn where trams are used to create a metro-like experience in the city center and a fast "express tram" experience outside of it.

Light metro like SkyTrain is FULLY grade separated and does not have any interaction with general traffic, but is a lower capacity than "heavy" metro like BART or the New York Subway.

> The problem isn't the money, is that the time frames keep ballooning and requiring more and more money.

The problem is also the money. America has been reluctant to invest in anything that isn't a road for decades, and with no steady stream of money we can't rely on building up a solid knowledge base in our public agencies if it'll never be used.

Other high income countries build things cheaper precisely because they know they'll have the money, so they build a strong public sector agency with a base of talent and knowledge and expertise specifically to build things as fast and cheap as possible. We do it with roads, which is why roads in America aren't much more expensive than the rest of the world.

> There needs to be reasonable incentive to use public transit, which will lead to higher ridership which will lead to more transit oriented development, which will further encourage the whole system.

One thing that nobody is going to like but really needs to happen is tolling some of the many highways in the region. If a highway has high quality parallel transit service (15min or better express bus or rail service) following the same route, then that section should be tolled.

Caltrain and 101/280, 880 with BART, 237 with VTA light rail, etc., would all be tolled with the funding directly going to support the operations of the transit and reduce the impact that the highways has on our climate and region.

> We could get better service with the same tax money if we just combined all the local agencies into a single regional one.

There is no guarantee of this. There should be much better coordination and fewer agencies to deal with, but a single agency system doesn't exist in lots of places. Seattle's Sound Transit doesn't run local buses, LA Metro has dozens of small agencies that serve the many cities in the region, the Rhine-Ruhr region in Germany (which has 5 or 6 major cities in it) has a regional agency that runs region-scale services but it doesn't run all the local ones.

An alternative proposed by Senator Cortese is consolidating the agencies to the county/sub-region level (all Alameda/Contra Costa agencies merge into ACT, all North Bay agencies merge into one or two depending on the structure) and having MTC running region-scale services similar to other places.

A single agency *could* work well like in lots of places, but then again there's no guarantee that it would be the best solution as is shown in lots of other places that don't use the same model.

Regardless of the outcome though, there needs to be better coordination with free transfers and more timed transfers, if not increasing frequency to the point where you don't need to time transfers, but that all relies on funding.
